newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian Metals - Chinese zinc arrives in Singapore.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - Chinese zinc arrives in Singapore.

text.p: Some 10,000 tonnes of zinc from China has arrived in Singapore and up to 10,000 tonnes more is probably on the way, base metal traders said on Friday.

"I'd say about 5,000 to 10,000 tonnes of zinc from China is already here," a senior dealer for a European metal trading company told Reuters. "There's probably another 10,000 tonnes on the way to Singapore."
A zinc dealer for a Japanese trading house said about "10,000 tonnes of zinc are now in Singapore warehouses."
"I heard another 10,000 tonnes will probably find its way here," he said.
Metal brokers Brandeis said in its daily review that large increases in zinc "are expected again in Singapore of 10,000 tonnes or more".
Traders in Singapore said they expected most of the zinc to be placed on warrant in the LME's Singapore warehouse.

The volume of zinc in the LME warehouse in Singapore has been rising steadily over the past few weeks. It reached 8,200 tonnes in the LME stocks report last Tuesday, up 2,025 tonnes from the previous Friday's report.
Zinc demand in the region was reported firm and the Chinese remained optimistic about the upside potential of the metal.
"I think the demand for zinc here is still strong," a Japanese trader said.
Three-month zinc was seen by regional dealers at 0300 GMT at around US$1,260/65 a tonne, up slightly from the late trade in London on Thursday of $1,260 a tonne.

One dealer said zinc prices on the LME will remain firm with a supporting line seen developing at $1,260/70 a tonne. There is also the prospect of a fresh push towards the $1,300 level because of expected strong demand in the second half of 1997.
But ample supplies of zinc for nearby months may hold down any spike in prices over the next few weeks, dealers said.
"I have a question mark whether prices can move up to $1,300 so soon," one said. "There's a lot of zinc in Asia right now."
Copper buying by China, on the other hand, appears to have slowed in the last week or so.

The Chinese are reported to have lifted most of the 16,175 tonnes taken from the LME's Singapore warehouse after copper stocks fell to 38,825 tonnes in the LME report last Tuesday from 55,000 tonnes reported last March 14.
"I'd think most of the stuff went to China," a European trader said.
Demand for the red metal in the region was steady, but unspectacular, dealers said.
"There's been a bit of buying this morning by the Chinese and the Japanese, but it's mostly regular stuff," one dealer said.

Traders said there has been some interest in Singapore copper warrants, but any impact on premiums will only be felt by next week. The presence of ample amounts of copper in the city-state will also cap any rise in premiums.
"It's difficult to say if the premiums can move up," a trader said.
Aluminium demand in Asia has also slowed sharply after brisk buying by countries like Japan and Indonesia over the last month, although premiums were holding at their current high levels.

"The market has calmed down," an aluminium dealer for a European trading house said. "I know there is no business going on. People are now covered for the second quarter. What they need, they already have."
Premiums in Japan were still seen at around $80 a tonne while those in Indonesia reached $90-$95 a tonne CIF Jakarta, traders said.
